utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Your Honour, Mr. Nicholas Koumjian, case manager Ruth Karper, and I appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Branko Lukic with Mr. John Ostojic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And once again, a special welcome to our witness, Mr. Murselovic. You may proceed with the cross-examination, and the Chamber decided to ask you kindly not to step over your own time limit set yesterday, half an hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good afternoon, Mr. Murselovic. I hope I won't torture you for very long today. I hope we'll be able to wind up quickly. Let me, without much further ado, start with the questions. On page 34, line 5 of Monday's transcript, you say that the Crisis Staff issued an ultimatum that all weapons should be surrendered, and that the soldiers should surrender themselves to Serb authorities, the context is the conflict in Hambarine. Can you tell us whether this was an ultimatum or an announcement, and what would be the difference?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an ultimatum. An ultimatum that the perpetrators of the incident, as they said, should be handed over. If they are not handed over -- some of the names were mentioned -- they will suffer consequences. This was read out on behalf the Crisis Staff. It was read out several times throughout the afternoon that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, had there been any armed conflict after the takeover, that is, between the takeover and the Hambarine conflict? Were there any armed conflicts in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous statement, I mentioned the fact that there had been a lot of incidents. And I explained them in some detail. I told you where they happened and why they happened. This incident, however, became an introduction to what was to follow, because a request had been made that all the weapons should be surrendered to the Serb authorities, and that the participants should be handed over to the Serb authorities. So it is true that there had been incidents before, but they were in relation to something completely different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this not constitute an attempt to resolve the conflict in a peaceful way?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was an attempt to find a peaceful solution to the problem, but as I said, there had been many incidents in the area before. Quite a few people had been killed, taken off the buses and killed. Ordinary citizens who had nothing to do whatsoever with incidents, so this kind of ultimatum was a classical example of ultimatum which was designed to disarm the people and render them helpless. And it was easy to figure out what would follow after the ultimatum, what would happen to them. I must say that immediately after the ultimatum which took place, I think, on the 22nd or the 23rd, a terrible -- well, I cannot call it really a shelling, but artillery fire was opened from the surrounding fills on the village of Hambarine, and one could clearly see that the houses were being targeted indiscriminately. People panicked, of course, because up until that time there had been no destruction of property. The fire, as I said, was opened from all of the surrounding hills. We could hear the shells coming, in particular, from the Serb villages and the barracks. This shelling lasted I'm sure more than one day. And I also know that there were a lot of civilian casualties in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now turn to your situation today, and let us try not to compare it with 1992. Today, as the president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, can you issue orders to the military?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no authority whatsoever to issue any orders. And of course, including the military. I am a head of a parliament, and my authority is strictly defined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 7 of your statement of the 14th of December, 1997, last paragraph, you say the following: "About six weeks ago after the September 1997 election, I was in Prijedor with Ibro Beglerbegovic and Sead Cirkin. We wanted to discuss the results of the election. While we were walking through Prijedor, we were approached by the son of Dr. Kovacevic". Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember this. I remember it was outside the Mrakovica Cinema, in front of the house which belongs to the priest Ranko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was with you apart from these two individuals? Was there anyone else in addition to Mr. Beglerbegovic, Mr. Cirkin, and yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Priest Ranko was with us, on that occasion. I cannot remember his family name. He was very surprised. Our car was parked outside the Prijedor Hotel, and we left the municipality on foot. And I saw priest Ranko there. He's actually my neighbour, and we started an informal conversation. I asked him: "You see, neighbour, we have built up this temple." The area was really nicely done after the previous destruction. And I said: "Do you know who financed most of this orthodox temple?" And he said that I know that you gave a lot of money, too. And I said: "Do you know who gave most of the money?" And he said: "I can't remember but I have it written somewhere." And I said: "It was Mr. Asef Kapetanovic who made the largest contribution," and there was a lot of talk around the town that it was Mr. Asef Kapetanovic who contributed most to the construction of the orthodox church. I must say that I put in some money, too, but not half as much as Mr. Kapetanovic. And I said: "Well, dear neighbour, why -- how come that you never mentioned that Bosniaks participated in the construction of this temple?" And he said: "Well, there was no opportunity for me to say this." And then I said: "See, I will probably be coming to Prijedor more often, and I would really be glad to hear you mention this fact." So we remained engaged in conversation for a while. And at one point in time, Dr. Beglerbegovic was approached by a young man whom I don't know and it was from their conversation that I learned that the young man was the son of Dr. Kovacevic. He simply wanted to speak to Dr. Beglerbegovic, to see whether he would be willing to appear as a Defence witness for his father. This, however, did not last very long. And we were soon joined by the wife of Sead Alajbegovic. I don't remember her name, but I know that she is a Serb. So this conversation finished after about 10 minutes, and we went back to our car. This is all I can tell you about this particular incident. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cirkin was with you also. Is he a former JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is. He was an officer of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he organised people in Kozarac for armed combat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I heard that during the war. He joined the war at one point in time, and I remember seeing him in Travnik a couple of times. He was a member of the SDA, and at the time, was one of the leading members of this party. He participated in a number of negotiations, and me and Dr. Beglerbegovic were representing the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know that he was an officer, and I know that he was allegedly in Kozarac before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you are currently a member of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the programme of this party envisage the solution of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of the programme of this party, as its name suggests, is a struggle for the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to keep the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina together. It is the platform of this party that many things should be regulated and resolved at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Part of this programme is also the idea that Bosnia and Herzegovina should constitute a single, unified, economic and political space. The party is also in favour of strengthening the central state bodies of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because we believe this division to be an unnatural consequence of the Dayton Accords. And the situation does not seem to be tenable. Let me illustrate this with an example: The town of Prijedor remained in Republika Srpska. The town of Sanski Most and the town of Kljuc remained within the federation. In the past, hundred years ago, this constituted a single area, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Bosanski Novi, being part of one and the same region, which was called the Prijedor district. The population of these towns are naturally linked with Prijedor. Now, these links have been severed, and nothing functions properly. The Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina advocates an establishment of a number of regions which would constitute economic and political holds. These regions should be multiethnic. A project has been designed to this effect, a project called "the regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina" which has partly been implemented. There has never been a slogan that Republika Srpska should be dissolved. We are in favour of dissolving both entities as such, that is both the federation and Republika Srpska with the purpose of strengthening the state institutions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you testify here that you were opposed to the centralisation which was conducted in the previous system in the past?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that attempts at one point in time were being made to centralise the area in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is still the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come that you are in favour of one centralisation and against another centralisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can spend a lot of time discussing this issue. I'm sure you're aware of these problems. Today, in Republika Srpska, attempts are made to retain the situation as it is. There is still a number of graffiti all around the town which read: "This is Serbia, stomp on Bosnia" and similar slogans. If you pass through a number of towns in Republika Srpska, you will come across some even very indecent graffiti, such as Serbia in my heart, and Bosnia -- now I don't want to use the expression that is used in this graffiti, but it describes a certain body part. So this kind of graffiti can be seen all around Republika Srpska. There is constant opposition to the regulations and laws which are designed to govern the life on the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am in favour of a body at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina which would bring all these institutions together. I am referring in particular to the bureau for borders and similar organs. Entities are still behaving as states, and in this post-war period, there is a tendency to have Republika Srpska function as an independent state with independent -- independently functioning state bodies. They even had, at one point in time, a Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as you know, whereas as far as the federation is concerned, there has been a strong tendency to identify the federation with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is equally wrong. These two entities are equal and are part of the state which is called the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't go too much into these details. It's easy to read in a judgment of the constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina where it is clearly stated what is a state and what is not a state. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Prijedor today, is there a multiparty -- multinational police in force?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peace agreement was signed in December 1998. On behalf of Republika Srpska, this framework agreement was signed by the president of Republika Srpska at the time, Mr. Poplasan [phoen], prime minister Milorad Dodik, and minister in the government of Republika Srpska, a person from Prijedor. I don't know what his function was. On behalf of the UN, this was signed by Elizabeth Wren [phoen], and the commissioner of the IPTF. And it was stated and defined when and how the police of Republika Srpska should be restructured and become a multinational police force. This, according to the agreement, should have been completed in the following way: 37 per cent Bosniaks in the police force in Prijedor, because the agreement envisaged that it should reflect the results of the 1997 elections. And at the time, this was referred to -- according to election results, the minority votes should also be reflected. So 37 per cent. If it is multiplied by the number of policemen in Prijedor, then this would be about 270 policemen of Bosniak ethnicity. So far, this process is evolving very poorly. I could speak at length about the obstruction on the part of the Serb authorities in the slow implementation of this framework agreement. Out of the 270 Bosniak policemen so far, in the police force, there is a total of 25 now employed, which is not even 10 per cent and does not -- it is not a satisfactory ratio provided -- which has been provided for in the peace agreement. So I don't know how we will arrive at such a multiethnic police force. And this part of the mission was not successful. Some employment has been achieved, but ever since 1990, the process has been very much obstructed. And in a more narrow body, with the UN people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only have a few more questions. Can you please tell me, have you ever been convicted of a crime?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never been convicted of a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever, in fact, convicted of false -- forging documents?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1995, I was indicted for not doing my job well, for negligence as a leader, but then this was withdrawn. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you charged of forgery?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this question was put to the witness, and he had clearly answered saying that he was not convicted. This is a repetition of the question. I'm not in the habit of disturbing my learned friend, but I take this position now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dismissed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have resolved the issue of 1997. Today, are there any proceedings against you that are in progress?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... An answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer the question? I'm asking the same question as I have done previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just refreshing his memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you charged with forgery?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been convicted -- accused yet. I will try to make things clear. It is a rather strange, ridiculous thing. It has to do with issuing town planning conditions in -- which has to do with my own property. And it appeared on the basis of the charges which was, in fact, a very ridiculous act that I, myself, forged my own documents. And regardless of that, of whether I forged this or not on my own plot of land, on my own property, town planning conditions that mean absolutely nothing. Town planning conditions represent a document, according to which building is possible on a particular site. But I am the owner of that site, and I received a building permit for a building which I'm continuing to build, a building which I started building in early -- as far back as 1990. So I have all the necessary papers. I received the building permit, and I believe that this has already been resolved, because I have the right to build a building on the basis of a design provided for by the town planning institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you owner of that land or are you only -- have the permit to use it for a lasting period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, I have the right to use it in a lasting fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a lot of overlapping. It is very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I received all the necessary papers for building that establishment. I don't think I will have any problems in Prijedor following this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would only like to have it put on record that in response to a question on page 11, line 6, a question whether he is owner of that land or only has the right of using the land, the witness answered that he was only able to -- that he had the right to use this land in a lasting fashion, permanently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I clarify this point. The entire land under -- in the socialist community and these laws have not changed. The land in town has been nationalised, and no one, absolutely no one, is owner of that land. In the villages, yes, they are owners. But in the city as such, in the town as such, the land has been nationalised and no one has the right to ownership but to use the land permanently while a building exists on that plot of land. But the land belongs to me in the sense that I'm able to use it, and I have the advantage as user of the land and as user of the buildings on that land, to have an advantage whereas -- in regard to any building activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you just receive an approval for building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have this approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Any longer questions on this issue. The witness before us is a witness and cannot be regarded as an accused here. He answered very clearly on the question, and this is an issue not to be resolved here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I have no more questions, Your Honour, and this was just a line of questions challenging the credibility of this witness. And I have finished for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What about re-examination conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Re-examination will be very brief, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, could you clearly state to the Court whether Mr. Milomir Stakic was at any stage the president of the Municipal Assembly before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milomir Stakic was never president of the assembly of the municipality of Prijedor. He was elected vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor following the 1990 elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I recall correctly, you said that Mr. Stakic was the president of the all-Serbian municipality. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In February 1992, when the Serbian deputies, representatives of the SDS party, well, they formed the Serbian assembly. And at that assembly, they elected the Serbian assembly of Prijedor. And in that assembly, Milomir Stakic was proclaimed president of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, after the takeover in April 1992, did Mr. Stakic become the president of the Crisis Staff? That was your position; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milomir Stakic became president of the Crisis Staff, and as such, he appeared in the press and signed all sorts of documents as president of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware, after the takeover, when the Crisis Staff was functioning, whether they adopted the rules of procedure or the municipal statute which was referred to you by the Defence yesterday, whether they worked according to that or that they functioned according to those rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the rules of procedure were or their statute as you say. I did not go to their assembly, nor was anyone invited apart from members of the SDS. I don't know how they functioned as a Serbian municipality of Prijedor. The Serbian municipality of Prijedor was a ridiculous thing as far as I was concerned because there were Bosniaks and Croats there, too, not only representatives of the SDS, but representatives of all other political parties, because, for instance, in the case of the Reform Party of Yugoslavia, the League of Communists, the Democratic Socialist Alliance and so on, and my party as well, and the youth party, the socialist youth, we all took part in the elections together. There were Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks, all these people took part in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when the Crisis Staff was functioning after the takeover, it was the all-Serbian party which was in authority?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Only Serbs were represented there. Serbs from the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, very quickly, Mr. Murselovic, you referred to some names yesterday when cross-examined by my -- by the learned counsel for the Defence. You referred to a person by the name of Senada Ramadanovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senadin Kapetanovic. He owned a pastry shop. His father was also owner of a pastry shop, and he followed in his father's footsteps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say -- to what ethnicity did he belong?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he survive the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him since May 1992, and I assume that he did not survive the camp because he never appeared in the last ten years. I know his family, his mother, his wife, his children. His mother came back to Prijedor. His wife and children, I think she is at present in Holland, but he never reappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another person, a name that you mentioned was Ziko Crnalic. If I recall, he, too, did not survive the Omarska camp. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not survive the camp. He was killed at the entrance to Manjaca. And the last time I told you about it. He was killed in my jacket, and I saw him dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, a lot of questions were put to you by the Defence with regard to Mr. Cehajic as to when he was the president of the Municipal Assembly. Is it correct that he was the president of the Municipal Assembly at the time there were many political parties existing in Prijedor and under the multiparty system?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Muhamed Cehajic was elected at the assembly after 1990. And this was an assembly where there were eight political parties, and Mr. Cehajic was elected as president of the assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas Mr. Stakic, when he was the head of the Crisis Staff and the head of his Serbian political party, how many political parties did function during that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, only one political party functioned, the Serbian Democratic Party, because they believed that only that party could lead the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, yesterday and today there were numerous questions on the role as it was under the statute of several persons. Let us just for a minute forget about statute law and so on. When looking back, which persons would you regard as most powerful persons in Prijedor after that what you called the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that the most powerful persons were the members of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality and the president of this Crisis Staff was Mr. Milomir Stakic. And it was from that period onwards, that is, from the takeover on and during the month of May, we considered him to be the most responsible individual, because he made a lot of public appearances over the radio and in the media, and also because he was the president of the Prijedor Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you give us some other names of persons in power in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention Dr. Kovacevic, Slavko Budimir, who was the secretary of the secretariat for national defence; Simo Drljaca, the chief of police. Then there was Mr. Kuruzovic, Slobodan Kuruzovic, who was involved with the Territorial Defence. He was the one who asked that the weapons be surrendered. We knew him from the media. So out of these people who appeared there within the Crisis Staff, as an executive body, they would have been the most responsible individuals. But I should not forget Mr. Srdjo Srdic, for example, who was a deputy to the assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina once. But these five or six individuals were persons who in my opinion -- yes, there were also the people who were members of the military leadership such as Mr. Radmilo Zeljaja, the commander of the garrison, and the town of Kozarac was at one point in time renamed and called Radmilovo, because of the merits of Radmilo Zeljaja. But I'm not sure about that. This is what we heard while in detention in the camp and while we were aware as refugees. I actually never saw these people such as Radmilo Zeljaja and other military men and I actually didn't know much about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Mr. Arsic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Arsic was also with this military structure. What kind of role he had there, I don't know. But both Mr. Arsic and Zeljaja were mentioned as individuals responsible in this sphere because they were commanders of the brigades which were established at one point in time in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There is now a short videoclip prepared. If you could be so kind to look careful on this video if you could identify one or the other person. And if so, then please ask for a stop or rewind, whatever is necessary. It is videoclip we saw already. It was Exhibit Number --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: S10, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S10. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see very clearly, but I think that this person here -- the image is very blurred, I'm afraid. I don't know Mr. Arsic. I cannot recognise him. You can go on with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was Mr. Stakic a moment ago standing to one side of the speaker. I believe that this is him. Actually, this is the first time that I'm watching this tape. The lady here who also spoke, I don't know her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this video. Do you know for sure where this video was taken? Could you identify the environment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as they said, it was taken in a village, but I don't know the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to members of the Crisis Staff, you mentioned the name of Mr. Drljaca. Can you please explain in short -- in your statement of 1997, page 3, English version, fifth paragraph, you just said: "He became the chief of the police." Can you please tell us, who is responsible therefore that he became the head of the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb municipality of Prijedor was responsible for that, because they appointed him to this post sometime in February. Up until then, he was a lawyer who worked at the centre for elementary education and had nothing to do with the police as far as I know, had no connections with the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In your statement of 2002, English version page 3, paragraph 7, you said: "He was foreseen to be head of the police in the Serb municipality."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a development from being head of the police and then head of the police in the Serb municipality, or why did you make the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because once the multiparty system came into existence, that is, after the elections, it was agreed that the chief of police should be Mr. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Hasan Talundzic, which he was. After the proclamation of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor sometime in February 1992, Mr. Drljaca was appointed the head of the police of the Serbian municipality. He was appointed to this post by the Serbian municipality of Prijedor. At the same time, Mr. Milomir Stakic was promoted and became the president of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, leave aside the statute, can one say that Dr. Stakic was the boss of this head of police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one can, because Mr. Stakic was also the president of the Crisis Staff, and the chief of police was a member of the Crisis Staff also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To whom was Dr. Stakic subordinate, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to whom he was subordinated. As far as I know, in Prijedor -- actually, I don't know to whom he would have been subordinated in Prijedor because after the takeover, there was neither de facto or de jure authority or individual who would be above Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You recall this in your testimony here and the basis of this formed your statement of 1997, English version, paragraph 1 on page 4. You ask for the future of your small business, and then, I quote: "He, Dr. Stakic, promised me to find out in Banja Luka and inform me through his secretary Mika. Mika is still working there, and I was never informed whether the small business continued with work." Why do you believe or do you know Dr. Stakic had to go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand. This is the secretary. But what is -- we are still in the context, who is superior and who is subordinate. Was there a special role that, for example, one could get the impression that orders would be obtained from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understood when Mr. Stakic told me: "I don't know what is going to happen, I don't know whether you will be working at all. But now, I'm going to go to Banja Luka now at 10.00 to get some information there. And I will then inform you." According to what we knew, which was logical, the body in question in Banja Luka was the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. And there are documents that I had the opportunity to see. I actually have these documents, which indicate that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region was sending reports -- sending documents to Prijedor and cooperating with the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. However, at the time, I was not aware of the way it functioned and how it worked. And Mr. Stakic said that he was going there to get some information, to get some instruction in Banja Luka. At least, this is what I understood him to mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned documents. Do you have still these documents in your office, your apartment, or somewhere else? You shouldn't tell us where it is --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I have a document of this kind here on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Today, here?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have these documents. I have them here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you would be so kind, and with the assistance of the usher, present this document on the ELMO. Can you please read out this document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the upper corner, we read: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Autonomous Region of Krajina. Banja Luka Crisis Staff. Number: 03-531/92. June the 12th -- I'm sorry, June 22nd, 1992. "To be delivered immediately to the president of the municipal Crisis Staff: At this session held on the 22nd of June, 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka reached the following decision: All leading positions, and the positions which are likely to receive important information, for the purpose of guarding public and state property at all locations which are important for the functioning of the local economy may be filled only by Serbian personnel, Serbian staff. This concerns all publicly owned companies. Share holding companies, state institutions, and public companies, ministries of the interior of the army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Likewise, employees of Serb nationality who have not confirmed this in a plebiscite and are not yet clear as to the idealogy, that the only representative of the Serbian people is the Serb Democratic Party cannot be in these positions. Paragraph 2: The deadline for the implementation of the decision stated in Paragraph 1 of this decision is Friday." I think that the date reads 26th of June, 1992, until 1500 hours. By that time, the presidents of the municipal Crisis Staffs are required to submit relevant reports to this Crisis Staff. Failure to comply with the above decision entails automatic dismissal of officials in charge. "Paragraph 4: This decision shall take effect, and there's a text that I cannot read. And shall be published in the official gazette of the autonomous region of Krajina. "President Radislav Brdjanin." And in the upper corner here, you can read in Latin script: "Decision implemented." This can be found on the same page, but there is -- this copy I have it at home, and this is just a photocopy, so it's on two pages. On this other page, we read the following text: "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Autonomous Region of Krajina, municipality of Prijedor Number 02-111-236/92. Date: 23rd of June, 2000 [sic]" At the session of the Prijedor Crisis Staff held on the 23rd of June, 1992, it was decided that we submit to you the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina for the purposes of its implementation. Attachment: Decision. Signed: President of Crisis Staff, Milomir, Dr. Stakic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the Court's information, I believe at least the first page, this is an exhibit that has already been translated. I have to check whether it's identical. I think we have the other one translated also, so at the break we can bring those down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How shall we proceed with the document? To be on the safe side, I regard it as necessary, at least, to have copies of both documents and those be brought to the registry to have these as exhibits, as formal exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can leave this to you if it be of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can the usher hand this document, please, first of all to the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Office of the Prosecutor may provide us after the break with copies, and then we will discuss the question of admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to explain to the Court, I think there's a -- some major procedures that -- regarding the evidence unit for anything like this. It has to be IIFed and ERNed as I understand it. We can check at the break. I don't think we have one identical with the writing on the top, but I'll check. If we have it already IIFed and ERNed, I suggest we just use the copy that we have; otherwise it will take some time to have this processed through the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary because there are numerous questions on the authenticity of such documents, and therefore we should be on the safe side that this is a document presented by us by the witness today. There should be no doubt at all. May I ask, do you have any other documents of this kind from former times, from 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I obtained this document after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the circumstances by which you obtained this document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An acquaintance of mine of Serb ethnic background brought this to me asking: "Have you ever seen a document like this"? Actually, "have you ever seen this document?" And I said yes. Actually, I didn't have this document but I said that I had seen it. And then he left it with me. He said: "I don't need it. I made a copy of this document. I'm leaving this to you." So I kept it. I remember having made several copies of this document which I then gave to some of my friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Some other relatively small questions to this issue: In your statement in 1997, English version, page 3, paragraph 5, the last sentence. You said there, referring to posters displayed, quote: "It was signed by Stakic on behalf of the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand this question very well. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I have to repeat slowly. I start with the third-last sentence: "It was announced in Radio Prijedor that the Serbs had to take over because politics of the SDA had led to bad economical situation in Prijedor. Something similar was written on posters displayed all over the municipality. It was signed by Stakic on behalf the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember now who signed it, whether it was the Crisis Staff or Dr. Stakic. Well, it happened quite a while ago, and I'm not sure -- I am hesitant about whether it was signed by Stakic. But Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff. And as such, he appeared in the press. He explained that announcement in the press. As you said, he spoke about why this was done through the mass media. And as being the most responsible person, and he explained this through the mass media why this was done. In view of all this, I felt that being president of the Crisis Staff, that his responsibility was the greatest. I cannot sincerely tell you whether it was signed by the Crisis Staff or Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Then just to continue, the next sentence reads as follows: "After the takeover, the curfew was implemented." Could you tell us, do you know by whom the curfew was implemented?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the explanations, all contacts with the mass media was in the hands of the Crisis Staff, which via the radio explained that the Crisis Staff had introduced the curfew, and stated how long the curfew lasted and also that no one was allowed to appear in the streets during that time. I never appeared in the streets then. I don't know who was in the streets at the time. It was stated in the announcement who was able and who was allowed to be in the street, the police. But the normal citizens could not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And a similar question, when describing on Monday the separation of non-Serbs at the Balkan Hotel in Prijedor, you said at a certain point that they ordered the Croats and Muslims to line up and separate from the Serbs. Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian soldiers who, in fact, brought us there. The Serbian policemen to be more specific, the reservist Serbian policemen who took us there in a certain sense. I told you who brought me there, that a neighbour took me from my home. His name was Ranko Vujasinovic. And there were about five or six -- I cannot remember the exact number -- of Serbian policemen who ordered us to line up and to separate because there were women there also, elderly people. And he said that Muslims and Bosniaks should separate. And we got up, and he took us to the exit and put us in the bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, a question far away from judicial questions: Looking now back, certainly you have put yourself the question, whom do you regard being responsible for what happened to you and the others in Omarska/Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whom I feel to be responsible. Well, above all, the leadership of the SDS, in particular, all the leading persons of that party. And those who, once they took over power, those who implemented directly and were responsible for all that happened following that, the establishment of the camps, the ethnic cleansing. And if I were to single out individuals, this was not something that could have been done by only a few people. But there are people who headed the whole process. And they included Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Stakic, Mr. Kovacevic, and Mr. Kuruzovic, and Mr. Srdjo Srdic, and all those who in some way were involved in the process and who were members of the Crisis Staff. I frequently wonder how this could have happened, how these people whom we knew and who were with us, who went to school with us, to high school with us, whom we associated with, how they could have done something like that. That is to say, arrest people without any grounds, abuse them, kill them. In Prijedor, there are villages where entire families had been killed. We have a book of persons -- of missing persons, and 3.270 -- less than 3.300 people. And I frequently wonder who were these people who could have killed women and children, people of over 80 and 90 were killed. I cannot find the answer why this happened. Then another question is the one that relates to prominent people in Prijedor. I cannot understand why all the more prominent doctors, Bosniak doctors, had to be killed, why Dr. Mahmuljin and Dr. Sadikovic and Dr. Pasic and Dr. Begic, why they had to be killed. Professor Cehajic. Professor Crnkic. Professor Mujagic, Sicer had to be killed. Why all the jurists, the lawyers had to be killed. The president of the Court, Mr. Seric, Kerenovic, Staric. The prominent craftsmen amongst whom Mr. Crnalic Dedo, Crnalic Ziko who was with his son, Zdenkic, in the restaurant business. I will probably die before I know why these people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A totally different question: You knew Dr. Stakic before the so-called takeover and after the so-called takeover. And probably even later you met him again. Probably you can later on tell us a little bit about this. But was there any change, significant change, in the personality of Dr. Stakic you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Dr. Stakic for the first time in early 1990 when the assembly was being established. I used to see him in the assembly. I saw him in the municipality. I saw him after the takeover of power when I encountered him in Mr. Cehajic's office as president of the municipality and of the Crisis Staff. I don't think Mr. Stakic changed much. Perhaps he had some more hair on his head ten years ago. He was fairly bald even at the time. Perhaps he was slimmer then. But generally speaking, he didn't change much, except perhaps that he lost some more hair. Well, we have all changed in a span of ten years. Many things change in that period of time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the personality? Did you regard him as a calm person, or especially sharp person? Have you ever met a person being, for example, the client of Dr. Stakic? Have you heard about his work before? What person was this in relation, yeah, to others you know? You said you met him in the street, in your restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never really heard of him as a doctor from his patients. He was a young doctor, and he was not employed in the town of Prijedor. I think that he worked in a dwelling called Omarska about 20 kilometres, 25 kilometres, between Prijedor and Banja Luka. Personally, I can say that when he was elected president of the assembly, I can say that he was a young doctor, modest. He seemed rather subdued. And he did not speak often at the assembly, and I don't remember whether he took the floor often or whether there was any manner that he was especially one could identify with him. But until the takeover of April 30th, until then, I thought of him as a modest, young physician. I could not imagine that he could have been the one to become president of the Crisis Staff, and then under his supervision, to have all those things happen. I considered him to be a rather modest person who was rather inconspicuous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, far from all legal terms, do you regard Dr. Stakic as responsible for that what happened in Omarska, Keraterm, Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe him to be very responsible. I say this personally. Not only Dr. Stakic, but also other people. But I considered him to be amongst the most responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this context, you mentioned -- and this was not referred during the -- your statement here -- the name of Suljo Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the father of my school friend Alija Ganic, along with Safet Ramadanovic. And as I found out later on -- actually, I did see him dead. He was also in Mujo's room. And in the toilet, he had -- he suffered from a stroke or a heart attack. I'm not quite sure. Nevertheless, he died there, and he was dead. And he was in our presence. And we took him out. Someone took him out from our room. And a similar case, Mr. Safet Ramadanovic experienced a similar fate. And he, too, was taken out of our room. He had died. And as far as we learned later on, they were the only two who were taken to Prijedor and buried at the local cemetery there. And then the propaganda and Serb press wrote that they were the only two persons who died of a natural death in Omarska which, in fact, made us laugh. But these were people who were singled out, that they were taken from Omarska, and that they had died a natural death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In your statement of yesterday, you mentioned a person that was now, in 2002, 2001, a guest of yours. And you said, I quote -- unfortunately I have not a pagination. But at 16.58, you said, I quote: "And unfortunately, as a Croat, he survived Manjaca, Omarska, and now he lives in Rijeka. Otherwise, he is married to a Serbian woman." Do you know the name of this person and the address? We can do it in private session. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecutor please during the break to show the documents to the Defence that then later on, the documents given by Mr. Murselovic can be submitted to the registry. We have a break now until 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Let's stay, first of all, in open session. A totally different question is the following: Was there any special financial society you were aware of the only possibility to make any kind of financial transactions, especially in Prijedor? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, the only institution which did the so-called financial transactions was the service of social -- social accountancy service, the SDK. All money transactions were done through the SDK. And the payments were done towards the accounts of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know which month it was, either March or April, but a decision was made at the time that the payments should be made and the Giro account numbers were changed to the budget of the autonomous region of Banja Luka. This was prior to the takeover of authority by Serbs. And I think that as far as my company's concerned, I think I only made one payment, maybe in April or May. Actually I'm not sure whether I made any single payment to that account. But I know that all Giro account numbers were changed, and that a request was made that the institution for financial transactions of Bosnia and Herzegovina be dissolved and that all payments should be made through Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now go, for a moment, in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement during the cross-examination yesterday, you mentioned Simo Miskovic and he was the president of the SDS and seeing him regularly in Prijedor today. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other persons you regard -- it's the wrong question. Any persons you regard as responsible for that what happened in Prijedor in former times living now still or again in Prijedor? And could you quote some names?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. (redacted) is in Prijedor. I believe he's now working as a deputy head master of an elementary school. I see from time to time quite a few interrogators from Omarska, (redacted) or (redacted) as we used to call him, who used to be the chief of the crime department. I also see (redacted), who is now working at the national park and was one of the interrogators in Omarska. I also see from time to time the people who interrogated myself. I mentioned the name of (redacted) (redacted) for instance. There are still quite a few people, people who participated in to a certain extent in the events in Prijedor and who are still living in Prijedor, but are not active members of the Serb Democratic Party, for example, nor are they active in the political life in Prijedor in general. For instance, two or three months ago, several police officers who have some kind of war history, war background, such as Tomcic have recently been removed from the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you believe that the one or other person you mentioned before in the one or the other context would be available as witnesses for this Tribunal? Did you discuss the question whether or not to come as a witness to The Hague with other persons in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Bosniak are concerned, Muslims, that is, many of them have appeared before this Tribunal as witnesses in a number of cases, including (redacted) [Realtime transcript read in error (redacted), and the number of others. (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, it's necessary for the protection of persons to go once again in private session and redact the names just quoted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we formed a coalition, this Party for Private Initiative, and the former Socialist Youth Alliance. I received a sufficient number of votes as a Bosniak and as a representative of this party, and a young gentleman, a Serb from Ljubija, he also obtained a sufficient number of votes in the election. So the two of us were actually representatives of this movement. We always sat next to each other at the sessions. Unfortunately, I cannot remember his name. He no longer lives in Prijedor. I don't know what happened to him during the war. I know that he was a Serb from Ljubija. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] So the two of you were the representatives of this movement in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me clarify: I represented my party, and he represented the Socialist Youth Alliance. But we participated in the election together. We were together on the lists, and he and I, we obtained a sufficient number of votes at the election. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] You told the Chamber that you had been accused on several occasions of having persecuted Serb children. We're not quite clear on that. Was that in a school? What was the context of this accusation of persecution of Serb children?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you about what happened in the camp. We were being accused of all kinds of things in the camp, of hating Serbs, of wanting to kill Serb children. They did this at free will. They used abusive language in respect of us. They cursed our Muslim mothers. They called us names, which was all part of the attempt to humiliate this one person who used to work at the school when I worked there as well. The person who beat me, Mr. Marmat, when I told him that this was not true and that he should check it with his sister, he actually did it. And his sister, whose name was Borka, apparently clearly told him that this was not true. This young woman, this lady, still lives in Prijedor and she works at the Prijedor municipality. I often see her these days, and we are on very good terms. We have very friendly contacts. But let me just emphasise that in my small, private company, I had both Bosniak, Muslim, and Serb employees. Out of 13 or 14 employees of my company, the ratio was always 50/50. That was the principle that I respected in my work. I had, after all, guests from all ethnic communities, and it was perfectly normal to have employees from various ethnic groups. And even today, a lot of these people, Serbs, who used to work in my company still live in Prijedor, and I'm on very good terms with them. Let me mention Ms. Dragana Babic, Ms. Biljana, who now owns a private shop, a private restaurant actually, which is called Balkan Express, who always greets me very friendly even from a 10-metre distance because she used to work for me for about 10 or 15 years. Then Rasa Radovan, who is now working as the secretary at the local tennis club. So I'm telling you these names because all those allegations were malicious and the idea was just to humiliate me and to have me beaten. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] One more question: You told the Chamber that Dr. Stakic had received you in his office of the president of the Municipal Assembly, that he physically occupied this office when he received you. How did he behave towards you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His behaviour towards me was very correct. He received me. I enter his office. I was not alone. I was accompanied by a Croat whose name was Andrea Pavic, and then Mr. Huso Hadzic, and also a secretary from our party, Mr. Simatovic, who is a Serb. He was very friendly. Well, not friendly; it is -- he was in a hurry, I think. And I asked him: "What is all this supposed to mean?" But I could see immediately that he had changed office, that he had moved to the office of the president. You know, we, the insiders know which office belongs to the president and which one to the vice-president. So this was a surprise for me. But he, as I said, agreed to see me. He received me, and I asked him whether we were supposed to continue with our work and what it was all supposed to mean. And I said: "You wrote in your announcement that the SDA was leading this town into economic disaster and a state of confusion. I want to know what's happening with other political parties, what will happen with private businesses? Will people continue to be employed? Will there be fuel? Will there be goods? Will it be possible to buy things in the future?" And he said: "Well, I don't know what's going to happen. The situation is not good." And he also said: "It is now close to 10.00. I am going to Banja Luka where I hope to obtain all the necessary information, and I'll get back to you." That was on the 3rd or the 4th. I'm not sure about the exact date, but it was two or three days after the takeover. Of course, he never got back to me, nor did I ever see him again. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] You told us on several occasions -- actually, you alluded to your party, so your party is the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My party at the time was the Private Initiative Party. I must emphasise that I was never a member of the Party for Democratic Action, the SDA. And generally speaking, I'm of the opinion that parties should not be one-nation parties, that people can live together and can have their interests represented together in a multiparty system, in a multiethnic system. And I believe, as I believed at the time, that one-nation parties will bring us no good because after all, we were a mixed community. I had a very small company, a very small business. Half of my employees were Serbs and half were Muslims. So it was my duty -- I felt it as my duty, as my obligation, not to join any national party because by doing so, I would be offending my employees. And I must also tell you that representatives of all political parties visited my restaurant and they were always well treated, well served, pay their bills regularly. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] You're now president of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I am the president of the local Prijedor assembly. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Can you tell us how you managed to be appointed to this office? Was it through an election?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1997, after the election, after the second multiparty election, but the first election which took place after the war, at the beginning of 1998, since it was necessary to have the leaders installed in their offices and to have a multiethnic leadership within the municipality, this whole process was supervised by OSCE, the European Organisation for Cooperation and Security. We called it OSC. And negotiations were conducted in the presence of the OSC who were representing the international community. There were regulations which requested us to have all political parties participate in the government since at the time we, Bosniaks, had about 37 per cent of votes as a result of the election, we made an alliance, a coalition. All of such parties, all Bosniak parties, including my party, the SDA, the liberal party, and another party which I cannot remember at the moment which was based in federation but had its branches throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina also of liberal province. We wanted to create a Bosniak front together. And as such, in this coalition, we obtained 37 per cent of the votes. As a result of the division of power following the elections, we got the post of the president of the Municipal Assembly, the vice-president of the Executive Board, and the secretariat for general administration and social services, as it was called at the time. So these posts went to us. This entire process was monitored by OSC, and the whole assembly had to vote on this. There were 65 deputies in the assembly at the time, and we tried, with some people from the SDA who were, after all, the most powerful fraction of this Bosniak alliance, to cooperate. But this didn't work because of the opposition of Serb parties. But at any rate, I was finally elected, as a Bosniak, to the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly. Two more Bosniaks are also elected, but they were not deputies to the assembly. We appointed them to the Executive Board as professional staff. At the time, this Executive Board still functioned. However, at the 2000 election, we were together again. We had a coalition once again, but we obtained 21 to 22 per cent of votes. There was another Bosniak party, also multiethnic party, which was with us, the SDP, or the reformed League of Communists now called "SDP." Only one of their deputies obtained enough number of votes, and we had seven deputies. But the assembly had only 31 deputies. Pursuant to an order of the OSC, who wanted to have this number of deputies increased, a new law on local government was passed, and a clear distinction was made between the parliament and the executive authority. And it was from a local Serbian party, SNSD, the president of this political party is Mr. Dodik, a famous politician who at the time was the president of the government, the prime minister, that Mr. Nada Sevo was elected mayor. And since the rules provide that in cases of one ethnic group obtaining more than 20 per cent of the votes, they have to have one of these two most important functions, and that is how I was eventually elected president of the local parliament, that is the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Other officials, other public servants, were subsequently elected, that is, the secretary of the assembly, the deputy or the vice-president, and the secretary of the secretariat. All political parties participated in the division of power this time so that the office of the vice-president went to the SDS. And representatives of minor political parties also got certain departments. So the idea was that everybody should participate in local government, and this is still the case today. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for clearing up these points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before giving the floor to Judge Vassylenko, I just want one clarification. You answered to a question of Judge Fassi Fihri about your meeting with Dr. Stakic in the office there. You said, I quote: "You wrote in your announcement that the SDA was leading this town" and so on. To which document do you refer here? Did you see this document? Was it signed by Dr. Stakic when you say "your announcement"? Could you please explain a little bit this document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was an announcement made public, announcements were actually posted throughout the town, and the local radio stations kept repeating the contents of the document every half an hour or so. And it was stated in the document that the SDS had overtaken power from the SDA, because it could no longer watch the SDA leading the municipality to an economic and political chaos. And for that reason, they took over power, and it was clearly stated that this was done by the SDS, and the paper was signed by the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor. I don't think the signature of Stakic was there; but since Stakic spoke about the -- and explained the announcement in the press and on the radio stations, it was only natural that he was president of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor. No one doubted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, you said: "You wrote in your announcement at that point in time." Was this rejected by Dr. Stakic, that you said "you wrote in your announcement..."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't reject that at all. He said: "We did this," and then he mentioned that the power had been seized without any violence, they said, and without any bullets fired. And at any rate, he -- one could sense from the talks one had with him that he was -- stood behind the announcement and that he had moved to the office of the president of the assembly. He felt like the president, and he was also elected president of the Serb assembly of Prijedor. There was no question about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it. He said: "I don't know -- I cannot tell you anything. I will go to Banja Luka. I will find out, and I will let you know." These were his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional clarification. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have some questions to the witness. Mr. Murselovic, during today's cross-examination, you referred to a list of more than 3.000 persons who disappeared during the conflict. What is the status of this list? Who is included in this list? Is this the number of people who disappeared in the whole municipality or only in Prijedor? This number of people disappeared being the prisoners of concentration camps or in conflict in total?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if this will assist the Court, but I will tell the Court that we have the book, and we also have statements from the authors of the book about how it was compiled, just for the Court's information for future reference. And it actually would probably be part of our demographic expert's report. I also add that I understand it's being revised, and we expect a revised copy in a few weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But I am interested, what is the status of this book? Who is compiling this book?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book was compiled by non-governmental associations of the Prijedor municipality, that was following the war within the federation, closely cooperating with the state commission for searching for missing people. On that list, all those who had disappeared, whose fate was unknown, were listed. People, men, women, children, Croats, and Bosniaks exclusively, who disappeared, all traces of whom were lost and who were registered with the state commission and who were searched -- for whom one searched. These people, Bosniaks, who were killed in fighting or as members of the Bosnian army, they are not in that list. They are included in that list. Only those about whose place of burial one did not know were on the list. And that list, that book, had 3.227 numbers, and the process of adding new names is continuing because there are still families who are searching for their members, for those people, and they do not know what happened to them. The situation was nightmarish and confused. Might I also add that so far, from that list, about 40 per cent of the persons have been identified and exhumed in a mass grave called Jakorina Kosa which is not far from the iron ore mine of Ljubija. In that mass grave, 374 bodies were exhumed, or 384. I believe it was 374 bodies were exhumed. Unfortunately, this was a secondary grave site, meaning that the bodies had been transferred from another grave site. And when the bodies were thrown into that hole, into that pit, they were thrown into the pit, and the remains of the use of dynamite could still be seen there on that grave site. Now, when the bodies were taken out, the grave was, in fact, closed by using dynamite. But the commission has its own principles, its own knowledge on the basis of which it's still searching for the missing persons. And this was the most massive grave site near Prijedor. It was very difficult to identify so many people. We were given the order to wait for the DNA analysis, not to rush the funerals. We asked from the state commission for missing people, because the international community asked that DNA analysis should be made from family members. And I must say that the bodies were in a bad state, and one could identify on the basis of clothing, of documents. This was only done for 20 per cent, because all these people were bundled in blankets, and now these bodies still stand. They have not been buried yet. They are in the Sejkovaca Hall in Sanski Most. And the anthropological process of identification are still in progress. It is very difficult to identify the bodies. The bodies have been mixed up. Some of them have missing limbs, because they were loaded on to dredgers. So it will be difficult to identify them. But the portion of persons who have been identified, they are on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you have a list of persons who were killed or died in the concentration camps or as a result of shelling of peaceful villages and towns?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that list of missing persons, and in the book, all persons who had not been buried and about whom one does not know where the burial site is, all these people have been listed there so that many people having disappeared from Omarska are in the book. And we found many -- several mass graves. When I say "we," I mean the commission searching for missing persons which cooperates with The Hague Tribunal and the UN mission. We found quite a number of people from the mass graves about whom we know had spent time in Omarska. They have been found in a mass grave in Podvarcaska near Gornji Kamengrad from a mass grave, which was, in fact, a pit 27 metres deep. Bodies had been thrown into it. Many people have been identified, people from that mass grave. Then from another mass grave, which is -- which has fewer people in it. This mass grave was found in the area of the Serbian part of Bosanska Krupa. This is also another inaccessible pit which was covered by garbage and closed up. It was, in fact, a cave. And nevertheless, the bodies have been exhumed. And quite a lot of people have been identified, and they are in that book, too. The book is still being worked on, and names of missing persons are added to it. For some of them now, we know that some of them have been exhumed and buried. Between 1.600 and 1.700 people have been exhumed. About 1.300, 1.400 have been identified, and they are all within the book of missing persons. I must say that many people were easily identified at the beginning. Those who were dug up in front of their homes. They were discovered when our people began to return to Hambarine, Carakovo, Biscani, and this whole area of the left bank of the Sana River in Kozarac. Because the family saw what happened. They knew where the dead bodies remained when they were running away. They were buried in shallow graves because there was not much time. And these people were easily identified. They usually had documents on them. But the process of identification in the mass graves, especially in the secondary mass graves, is a very difficult identification process and can only be done by DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: When did you for the first time became aware of the existence of camps and detention centres in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw this for the first time when I was arrested on May 30th and when I was taken to the Omarska camp. Then, I saw that everything had been carefully prepared. The people that I saw there, like Nezir Krak, for instance, well, he will often tell me that he had come on the 27th of May, and he told me: "Mursel, you should celebrate May 27th as your birthday, because you were -- they searched for you here on the 27th when we came to Omarska. They searched for you. They searched for Senad Ramadanovic. Someone called Cuka. I think his name was his Muhamed. He owned a pizza place, I think his name was Izetagic. They looked for Ilijaz Music, who was a professor. And he told me you should celebrate that day because some had gone that day, and you were not among them." I was released after my first arrest, and I was in Prijedor. And then I realised that everything was very carefully prepared in the camp, that there were guards around them, very well distributed around the camp. The next day, they would bring us a little bit of bread. The first few days, there was nothing to eat. And I must say that I saw the people who would bring the food to the camp, who work in the social restaurant of the iron ore mine of Ljubija. I used to know a person who I saw with my very own eyes, her name was Mara. She was, in fact, head waitress in one of those restaurants. I knew her because she was a colleague of mine in the restaurant business. Of course, I did not say hello to her. But food was well organised. It came on a daily basis. I explained what the -- what kind of food was served, but I must say it was very well organised before I came on May 30th. And I remained there until August 5th and 6th when I was transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you know how many camps existed in Prijedor municipality, and what was their capacity, let us say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what I heard from people who were coming, I found out that there was a camp called Keraterm, because some people from Keraterm were brought to Omarska. I was brought directly to Omarska. And I hadn't been in any other of the camps in the area of Prijedor with the exception of my trip to Manjaca, which is in the municipality of Banja Luka. So that I cannot say what the number of -- how many other camps there were. I know about Keraterm, Omarska. I don't know how many people there were in Keraterm. In Omarska, we knew what the number was there, because we counted the groups of 30 that would come and go. And usually, according to our own assessments and my own assessment, there may have been about 3.000 people there. It was of course impossible to count them all because people were scattered around in different places. But the average number was about 3.000. I don't think that anyone really knew what the exact number of prisoners were, because people were called and searched, looked for, who were not even in Omarska. So that they didn't keep very strict records about this. The guards called names at random, names of people whom they supposed were in Omarska, along with those who -- about whom they knew who had been interrogated and their presence was known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: When did arrests and consequent detention of Muslims start en masse in Prijedor municipality? Do you have some knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
