utterances.text: As far as I know, arrests en masse and people being returned home from work were going on throughout May 1992. And people told me that on the 26th and the 27th of May, they were detained in Omarska. I arrived on the 30th, which means that people had been brought there before. I don't know exactly when detention in Keraterm started, but I know that on the 30th, both on the 30th and the 27th, as people told me that they were in -- that they arrived in Omarska from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What -- in your opinion, what municipal board or officials ordered and organised arrests and detention of the people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. Besides, I think I have mentioned quite a few times during my testimony that the overall control over the town, the entire situation, both in terms of security, politics, and the military issues, was exerted by the Prijedor Crisis Staff. The Yugoslav People's Army was by all means involved. A civilian portion of Defence Forces was also mobilised, together with the police into the Serb army. But they were the main actors as far as taking people in custody, detaining them in camps is concerned. I think that the Prijedor Crisis Staff had overall control of the situation. They constituted a body that had the authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You have been detained in Omarska for -- since the end of May until the beginning of August. Did Dr. Stakic or other members of the Crisis Staff ever visit Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Dr. Stakic in Omarska. But I cannot say whether he came to Omarska or not. I didn't see him. As far as other members of the Crisis Staff are concerned, I don't know. I remember someone say that Mr. Drljaca used to come. I didn't see him either. But I must tell you something: I didn't try hard to make myself visible. I tried to remain as invisible as possible, because the situation was such that it was so easy to disappear overnight. So I remember seeing some people -- for example, I saw in the morning when the inspectors would come, I remember seeing some people from Banja Luka. And I remember seeing Mr. Dragosavljevic, the currently president of the Court who used to be a judge in Prijedor. These individuals were in charge of these proceedings. But after 30 days of my stay in Omarska -- actually, it was only after 30 days of my stay in Omarska, I was taken for interrogation. During this period of time I tried to hide as much as possible because I could see that it was very easy to get killed. I remember an incident which was widely talked about when a detainee was eating a piece of dry bread, and then Serbs told him, "enjoy your meal." His name was Hadzalic. And he said thank you, bujrum. And this expression,"bujrum," is commonly used in Bosnia in this context. It is a Bosniak expression, and it actually means please feel free to join me. I believe it is of Turkish origin. And they said: "Are you telling us bujrum?" And then they opened fire and killed him on the spot. It happened on the pista. So of course, in few of such situation, I didn't feel like saying hello to anyone. I tried to observe as little as possible, but of course, I ended up by observing quite a few things. It was not very smart generally speaking to speak up or to say anything. I remember a case of a butcher -- actually, a son of a butcher who lived in Partizanska Street. He knew one of the guards, and he said "hello" to him. He addressed him by his name, and he was taken out by other guards and killed on the spot. I think his name was Mejo. It was much more advisable to hide and to make one's self invisible, and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Earlier this year, to be precise, on 13th of January, you testified, English version, written testimony, page 3, paragraph 3: "As far as I know, there were no sessions of the assembly after the Serbs took over. After the takeover, all power was exercised by the Crisis Staff. There were press articles saying that Stakic was the head of the Crisis Staff. There was considerable information about the role and importance of Crisis Staff to the public." May I ask you to be more specific in regard of your assertion that all powers was exercised by the Crisis Staff? What had happened with the other municipal bodies? And what were the concrete powers or prerogatives of the Crisis Staff? Do you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the SDS took over, and the power was taken over, the way I described you with about 1.000 soldiers, people under arms who had completely blocked the town overnight, they set up checkpoints. And outside all public buildings and companies, Serb soldiers were posted. As for the high-rise buildings, snipers were placed on top of every skyscraper, and one could plainly observe that. Serb soldiers walked around the town, very often drunk and behaving improperly. All of the Bosniak and Croat leaders of local companies and institutions were turned Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. back from work. Some people, and some -- in some institutions, as far as I know, did go to work. But these people, according to their opinion, were harmless. They were not very important figures in the town. And according to their opinion, they were loyal to the Serb state. Then the curfew was introduced, which created an abnormal situation for the people around the town. Nothing functioned at the time, as far as I know. I don't know what the situation was in local companies, but many of them were closed. I was arrested for the first time some 20 days after that. Then I was arrested on the second occasion. Many incidents started taking place in the territory of the Prijedor municipality. And well, Your Honours, I owe you an answer. You asked me about the number of the missing persons in the municipality of Prijedor. These people -- this number concerns the entire area of the municipality of Prijedor. Rakovcani, Rizvanovici, Carakovo and so on and so forth. This is what I could tell you generally speaking about the situation in the town of Prijedor in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: In your statement I just quoted, you referred to "the considerable information about the role and importance of the Crisis Staff." Can you share with us your knowledge about concrete sources of such information?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A concrete source of information was the local newspaper, Kozarski Vjesnik, and the local radio station. Some of the information was quite funny, you know, after all of the incidents that had taken place in April and May. I think that very often they were asking for incidents. They wanted to have a good reason for incidents. And then I remember an article which was published one day in Kozarski with the title "Prijedor, a peaceful city." So I thought it was pretty ridiculous. Anyway, we obtained all local information from the paper Kozarski Vjesnik, and the local radio station, which is still operating in Prijedor. They broadcast regularly their news blocks, and the paper was published in the evening, Friday -- Thursday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the last question: What is your opinion? Due to what personal merits, qualities, activities, Dr. Stakic was elected as vice-president of Prijedor municipality before the takeover, and then became the president of Serbian assembly which was created by Serbs in Prijedor? And after that, he became the president of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor, after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first multiparty election, two most powerful political parties were the SDS and the SDA. Mr. Milomir Stakic was a rather prominent member of theirs, because he was relative young at the time and he was a physician. He worked in Omarska as a doctor. He worked in a place where his party obtained majority of votes. So it was perfectly normal for him, so young and educated, to be assessed by the party as the most agile of their members. He's from Prijedor, where the party obtained a lot of votes. And as such, he was nominated and proposed as a candidate by the SDS to the post of the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe it's only fair to give the possibilities for additional questions to the parties. The Defence? And if there are any questions, we should have a break before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we would like to use that right when we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: One question, Your Honour. Just a clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good. Then let us have a break. But before, let us resolve the last technical question as regards the document handed over by the witness. It is necessary to know, is this one document or are these two documents? They were fixed to each other. Did you ever have the document with the front and back side and make copies from this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's only one document, and you, as a witness, stand for this, that this is the front and the back side of the same document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this document has the number 404B. Any objections against the admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have objections. Authenticity. You know that it's altered, and that we can speak about it after the break as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have this document without this addition in our possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it's probably another document. We have only, once again for clarification, it has to be regarded as a document handed over during testimony by the witness present here. And therefore, it is, as such, admitted into evidence as 44B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have a suggestion regarding the document. I know that the rules require a translation, although there was a translation when it was read. We have basically the same document without the writing in the upper right. And I would suggest that the original that we have and the translation come into evidence as 4A or 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. We should proceed strictly separate and take care that we don't confuse the documents. If it's -- let's say a similar document, then this should go as 45A and 45B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine, yes. Again, the only difference I saw was the writing in the upper right. And this was -- my case manager gave me the 65 ter number somewhere. This is 65 ter 249. And just for the record, the English ERN -- it's a two-page document -- begins 00916505; the B/C/S ERN number stamped on it is 0063-3170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to receive an explanation from the Prosecution whether it's one sheet document as the witness said or two separate documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I cannot give a clear answer because what I have is what's printed out, and it's printed out on two sheets. The original would be in the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, it's a question of evaluation of evidence. And this new one, therefore, should go -- Madam Registrar, please take care. The first one, decision, goes in the B/C/S version as 45B, and in the English version as 45A. But due to the fact that the additional document probably is another one forming not part of the same document, and this has to be discussed, this document, where at least in machine writing you can read at the end of the document "Milomir, Dr. Stakic," and the number ends with 171, this goes in B/C/S as 46B; and in English, 46A. So I believe now a break is well deserved, and we start at 6.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Murselovic, we know it is very hard for you to go through such an examination through three days and still important questions at a quarter past 6.00. But nevertheless, I would ask you to answer the following question: Having thought about it carefully, the document you gave us in a photocopy, what you saw, as you said, as one document with a front side and a back side, was this also a photocopy, or was this an original, with an original signature on it, or some handwriting on it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I received was a single-paper document. On one side, the document of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Krajina; and on the other side, it was the response of the Crisis Staff to the municipality of Prijedor. I also received that as a copy. But when I photocopied, the photocopy machine can only photocopy one side, and then on another sheet of paper, the other side. I have that document, which on one side, is the document from the Banja Luka Crisis Staff; and on the other side of the same sheet of paper, on the same sheet of paper, the front and the back of the page. I didn't really pay attention to this. I think it was a photocopy. We had to send it out to many companies, to many institutions, many organisations in Prijedor. We had to send it out to about 50 or 60 different addresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who, in this case, is "we"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said "we had to send this document out to about 50 or 60 addresses."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. One had to send the document to many different addresses to Prijedor so that perhaps one copy reached one of the companies where I, too, received the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. And then can you remember the document you had in your hand, were there -- was there a stamp on the document on one side or on both sides? And can you remember the colour of such a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamps were on both sides of the paper. And as it was a photocopy, it was all black and white. I don't know how the original document appeared, how it looked, whether the stamp was in a different colour. I received it as a photocopy, and it was in white and black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And we can identify on the top of the page a name. You mentioned the name before. Was this also part of the photocopy, or was this name handwritten on this special copy you had, and do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the document on which it was said "decision implemented." And I know the person in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is the person? We go into private session. [Private session].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, by this line of questions, you have shortened our questions, so we'll have only a few. Thank you. Further cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I promised that I would not question you any more today. I have only a few very brief questions to put to you. Because of translation from English and into B/C/S, some things require further clarification. If you could explain to us what you had in mind when you said that Milomir Stakic was a very correct person when you met him after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to say -- I would like to say that he received me in that situation. It would not be correct to say that he refused to receive me and that he was rude or arrogant vis-a-vis me. He received me, together with my associates I said who were with me. This lasted only 15 minutes. We didn't even have time to have a cup of coffee. And by the very fact that he received me in that situation, I believe this to have been a very correct move on his part. He probably had other business to attend to. He said that he was in a rush to reach Banja Luka, and I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you never saw Stakic in Omarska, and that you only heard from others that Simo Drljaca had come. You heard that from others and you never actually saw him yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic, although he is from Omarska, I think he is from Maricka, he used to work in Omarska and live in Omarska. I don't know whether he actually did come. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your restaurant, was it operational following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that one of the restaurants, I had sold it in August. And I stopped working in 1991. As regards the snack bar, until my arrest, it worked only partly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last question: You said that the missing persons who have been listed in the book, that this applies to the whole territory of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this relate to the entire war period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 99 per cent of the cases, these were people who went missing in 1992 following the ethnic cleansing which was particularly widespread in 1992. There remained a certain number of Bosniaks, 4 or 5.000, who were also cleansed -- actually, expelled in the summer of 1995. In 95 per cent of the cases, the people who are on those pictures and the date of -- when they went missing is the date that has been clearly marked in the book. And in 95 per cent of the cases, these were people who had disappeared in 1992; in most cases, in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further examined by Mr. Waidyaratne: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you spoke about the elections in 1997 and in 2000 and thereafter; that is, after the Dayton peace agreements and other agreements. Did the agreements provide means for those who fled or had to leave Prijedor and who now live in other countries or in other municipalities to vote in these elections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people -- because this was organised by the OSC, many people voted in absentia, which meant that many people voted outside their place of residence of the time. In 1997, the number -- the number of Bosniaks who voted in absentia was almost 100 per cent. This was in 1997. In the year 2000, we did our very best to have several polling stations in the municipality of Prijedor. I must clarify some points. In 1997, those who insisted on coming to vote in Prijedor, voting was organised in Alisici between Sanski Most and Prijedor. There, a maximum of 150 or 200 people voted. But in the year 2000, we formed two voting places. Since the Serbian political parties reproached us for getting votes from bags [as interpreted], that this was organised by the international community. Because of this, we wished to have some polling stations in Prijedor itself, and we required people that had returned, then, to vote in their particular settlement, in their village. There was a voting place in Kozarac and another one in Hambarine. Not very many people from Prijedor voted then. About a thousand people voted all in all, compared to the number of Bosniaks who lived there before the one [as interpreted] and those who had the right to vote. This was a very insignificant number. But it was in our political interest to have people vote, to vote in their place of residence and to return to those places. In the year -- this year, when we shall organise the elections in October, general elections will be held then. We will do our very best to have as many people vote in the territory -- on the territory of their own local community, to have as many people to register in their place of residence in Prijedor. And this is a continuing process, to increase the number of returnees and the number of voters. However, I must say that even then, when the OSC was organising elections, people could vote in absentia. The headquarters were in Vienna; and by mail, the voters received voting lists, and they could vote in absentia. We hope that this year, regardless of the fact that for the first time the electoral commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina is organising the elections, we expect very many people to vote in absentia, although this has not been regulated in great detail because for the very first time, Bosnia and Herzegovina is organising elections. So we don't know how things will turn out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Mr. Murselovic. The document that you handed over today to the Court - you may explain this - could you tell as to when you received, when you got the document from this other person? Do you recall when?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the day. I received the document in the course of this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no other questions. Mr. Murselovic, I have to thank you indeed very much for your comprehensive insight you gave us in the development of Prijedor from 1990 until today in our effort to come as close as possible to the truth in our, not only mandate to be a criminal court, but also in our mandate to perform a peacekeeping mission here in The Hague. I thank you very much. And thereby, we adjourn and resume for the 17th session on Monday, the 13th of May, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
